paper_title: MixTok: Adaptive Visual Tokenization with Global 1D Tokens and Sparse 2D Refinement

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Efficient visual tokenization requires balancing representation compactness with the preservation of fine-grained image content. Conventional grid-based tokenizers allocate tokens uniformly across spatial locations despite non-uniform visual complexity, whereas compact 1D tokenizers aggregate global information but can struggle to preserve local details. We introduce MixTok, a hybrid visual tokenizer that combines a compact 1D global representation with sparse 2D tokens for local refinement. A content-adaptive router ranks candidate locations by refinement priority and determines the number of 2D tokens for each image under a target average token budget. At the highest-scoring locations, 2D token features replace the spatial features recovered from the 1D representation, and a shared decoder reconstructs the image from the resulting mixed features. On ImageNet 256 x 256, MixTok achieves highly competitive reconstruction and generation performance, with an rFID of 1.195 and a gFID of 1.95 at respective average budgets of approximately 128 and 131 content tokens per image.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Visual tokenizers compress high-dimensional images into compact latent representations that
support reconstruction and provide a modeling space for downstream generators [1–4]. A central
challenge is to allocate representational capacity efficiently: visual complexity varies both within
and across images, yet compact representations must retain the information needed for faithful
reconstruction and generation. This calls for tokenizers that adapt token allocation to image
content.
sections.content: Existing visual tokenizers typically represent an image as either spatial grid of 2D tokens or compact 1D latent sequence. Conventional 2D tokenizers preserve an explicit correspondence between tokens and spatial locations, enabling localized representations of structures and textures [1]. However, their uniform spatial allocation assigns the same token density to visually simple regions, such as smooth sky, as to regions containing intricate objects or textures, potentially wasting representational capacity. In contrast, 1D tokenizers aggregate information across the image into compact sequences without one-to-one spatial correspondence [2]. Although this global aggregation improves compactness, preserving fine-grained local details within short sequence remains challenging [5]. These complementary limitations motivate combining compact global representation with selectively allocated local capacity. Beyond spatial allocation, most existing tokenizers assign the same number of tokens to all images at given resolution, regardless of content complexity. This fixed per-image budget can allocate unnecessary capacity to simple images while limiting detail preservation in complex ones [6]. An effective content-adaptive allocation strategy should therefore determine both where local tokens offer the greatest benefit and how many tokens to assign to each image, coordinating spatial selection and per-image allocation under target average token budget. To this end, we introduce MixTok, which adaptively allocates 2D tokens for local refinement. Built upon off-the-shelf 1D and 2D tokenizers, MixTok first maps small set of 1D tokens into spatial feature map that provides base representation of the image. content-adaptive router then determines where and how much to refine: grid scorer ranks spatial locations by refinement priority, while top-p budget controller determines the number of selected locations from the resulting score distribution. The selected 2D features refine the 1D-derived base grid, and shared decoder reconstructs the image from the combined representation. This design retains the compactness of the global representation while allocating additional capacity to local details that require refinement. For downstream image generation, we employ two-stage MaskGIT [7] pipeline. The first stage generates the 1D base tokens, which guide the selection of refinement locations and the number of 2D tokens to generate. The second stage generates these selected 2D tokens, after which the shared decoder produces the image from the combined representation. On ImageNet at 256 256, MixTok achieves an rFID of 1.195 and gFID of 1.95 with respective average budgets of approximately 128 and 131 tokens per image, demonstrating high-quality reconstruction and generation with compact representations. Our main contributions are as follows: We introduce MixTok, hybrid visual tokenizer that combines compact 1D global representations with sparse 2D local refinement through spatial feature replacement and shared decoder. We develop content-adaptive router that jointly selects refinement locations and determines per-image token counts through learned spatial scoring and top-p selection under target average token budget. We extend MixTok to downstream image generation through two-stage MaskGIT pipeline and demonstrate its reconstruction and generation performance on ImageNet at 256 256.

sections.title:
2 Related Work
Visual tokenization. Visual tokenizers map images into compact latent representations for re-
construction and downstream generation [8–12]. VQ-VAE [13] learns discrete representations
by quantizing encoder features into codebook entries arranged on a spatial grid. Subsequent
work improves this framework through reconstruction objectives, model architectures, and quan-
tization schemes [14–17]. VQGAN [1] introduces perceptual [18] and adversarial objectives [19]
to improve reconstruction quality, while ViT-VQGAN [20] adopts Transformer-based encoders
and decoders [21] with improved codebook learning. MAGVIT-v2 [22] introduces lookup-free
quantization based on binary latent codes, enabling larger token vocabularies. These methods
improve the quality of spatial representations, but their fixed latent grids impose uniform token
density across image regions.
sections.content: Another line of work replaces spatial grids with compact 1D latent sequences. TiTok [2] uses learnable latent tokens to aggregate image information into short discrete sequence. TATiTok [23] extends this approach with text-conditioned decoding and simplified single-stage training procedure. In the continuous setting, MAETok [24] uses masked modeling and auxiliary feature prediction to learn compact, semantically structured representations for diffusion models. Beyond sequence compactness, SelfBootTok [25] separates global and local token groups and learns to predict local details from global tokens, allowing downstream generators to model only the global tokens. However, recovering local content solely from compact global representation may remain challenging when image-specific details are not adequately encoded in that representation. MixTok addresses this limitation by retaining additional 2D tokens at selected spatial locations to complement the compact 1D representation. Adaptive visual tokenization. Adaptive visual tokenization seeks to balance representation size and reconstruction quality by varying token counts or spatial allocation. One direction supports flexible per-image token budgets. FlexTok [26] learns an ordered, coarse-to-fine 1D sequence that supports reconstruction at different chosen lengths. Such flexibility enables variable token budgets but does not, by itself, specify how to select budget for each image. ALIT [6] adapts representation length through recurrent token allocation, progressively adding latent tokens to improve reconstruction. CAT [27] uses caption-based complexity assessment to select an image-dependent compression ratio. related direction adapts the spatial distribution or support of tokens. DQ-VAE [28] varies coding granularity according to regional information density, assigning fewer codes to smooth regions and more to regions containing fine details. GPSToken [29] represents image regions using parameterized 2D Gaussians with associated texture features, allowing token positions and spatial supports to adapt to image content. However, spatial adaptation alone does not adjust the image-level token budget to the overall information content of each image. In contrast, MixTok jointly determines where to allocate 2D refinement tokens and how many each image requires, assigning additional capacity according to the refinement needs of the 1D representation while maintaining target average token budget.

sections.title:
4.2 Content-Adaptive Token Allocation
The benefit of local refinement varies across spatial regions and images. When the 1D representation
already captures a region well, allocating additional 2D tokens provides limited improvement. For
reconstruction, MixTok therefore uses a content-adaptive router comprising a Reconstruction Grid
Scorer and a Budget Controller. The former scores candidate locations, and the latter uses these
scores to determine the refinement locations and token budget for each image.

Features obtained from the generated 2D tokens replace the corresponding base features before shared decoding. MixTok generates its hybrid representation in two stages: global 1D tokens establish base representation, which then guides the selection and generation of sparse 2D refinement tokens (Figure 3). The base grid lies in the image decoders feature space, whereas the 2D generator processes inputs in its token embedding space. To use the base representation as generation condition, we introduce an Embedding Adapter that maps the base features to spatial context embeddings: Hctx = A( F1D). Sparse 2D generation and decoding. fine-tuned Halton-MaskGIT [32] generates 2D tokens only in R, conditioned on class and the context embeddings at unselected positions. Sampling follows the Halton order restricted to R. Each generated token replaces its mask embedding with Etok(ti), while the context embeddings at unselected positions remain fixed. The generated 2D tokens are converted to decoder-aligned features and combined with the base grid using Eq. (9) to produce the final image. Generation training. To train the Embedding Adapter A, we decode the base features into images and re-encode these base reconstructions with the 2D tokenizer. The resulting tokens are looked up in the frozen pretrained Halton-MaskGIT [32] token embedding table to obtain regression targets for A. We then freeze and fine-tune the Halton generator using the 2D tokens of the original training images as targets, applying cross-entropy only to masked positions within R.

sections.title:
5.1 Experimental Setup
Dataset and metrics. We train on ImageNet [33, 34] 256 × 256 and evaluate reconstruction on
all 50,000 validation images using rFID [35] and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR). Released
tokenizer checkpoints are reevaluated with common preprocessing and metric computation. We
report gFID on 50,000 class-balanced samples per sampling seed using the ADM evaluator [36].
sections.content: Model configurations. Our main configuration combines TiTok-L-32 [2] (32 1D tokens) with LlamaGen VQ-16 [31] (a 16 16 2D grid and the shared image decoder). For reconstruction, the 7 fixed variant retains 96 2D tokens and the top-p variant uses approximately 96.1 on average. We also evaluate transferability using ALIT [6] and its VQGAN backbone. Training strategy. Starting from pretrained tokenizers, we first align the 1D features to the shared decoder space, then train with fixed refinement budget before fine-tuning with top-p allocation. The 1D encoder and quantizer remain frozen throughout tokenizer training. Detailed training and evaluation settings are provided in Appendix A.

5.2 Image Reconstruction
Reconstruction comparison. As shown in Table 1, MixTok achieves an rFID of 1.1950 and a
PSNR of 19.51 dB with approximately 128 content tokens on average. At a comparable token
budget, it improves rFID over both TiTok variants and One-D-Piece, while remaining competitive
with FlexTok and DetailFlow. Figure 4 shows that 2D refinement improves stripe patterns and
curved boundaries over the 1D base reconstructions.

sections.title:
5.3 Image Generation
As shown in Table 3, MixTok achieves a gFID of 1.95 with approximately 131 tokens. At a similar
token budget, it improves gFID over TiTok-S-128 from 2.00 to 1.95 while reducing sampling
rounds from 64 to 16. Compared with DetailFlow-32 at a similar parameter count, MixTok
achieves a lower gFID (1.95 vs. 2.63) with approximately half as many tokens and fewer rounds
(16 vs. 39). Under our single-image latency protocol, MixTok is 3.77× and 2.48× faster than these
TiTok and DetailFlow configurations, respectively. Starting from the same generated 1D tokens,
sparse 2D refinement improves gFID from 4.33 to 1.95 with eight additional sampling rounds,
demonstrating its contribution to generation quality. Figure 5 illustrates improved local details
after 2D refinement during generation. Quantitative results and sampling-round ablations are
provided in Table 9 and Appendix A.7.

5.4 Ablation Studies
Grid scorer. To evaluate whether learned scores identify effective refinement locations, we
compare the Reconstruction and Generation Grid Scorers with random, uniform, and gradient-
entropy rankings. We hold each image’s top-p budget K(x) from the Reconstruction Grid Scorer
fixed across all strategies, isolating spatial ranking from budget allocation. Uniform ranking
follows a predefined spatially dispersed order, while gradient-entropy ranking uses the Shannon
entropy of grayscale Sobel gradient magnitudes. As shown in Table 4, the Reconstruction Grid
Scorer achieves the best rFID of 1.1950. Using only 1D base features, the Generation Grid Scorer
also outperforms all tested heuristics, achieving an rFID of 1.3479 and a PSNR of 18.4776. These
results support learned spatial selection and show that distillation preserves useful refinement
priorities without access to 2D features.

sections.title:
6 Conclusion and Future Work
We presented MixTok, a hybrid visual tokenizer that combines compact 1D global tokens with
sparse 2D tokens to preserve local details. Its content-adaptive router determines both where
to refine and how many tokens to allocate to each image under a target average budget. The
resulting representation supports reconstruction and two-stage masked generation, achieving an
rFID of 1.195 and a gFID of 1.95 on ImageNet at average budgets of approximately 128 and 131
content tokens, respectively. Ablations and experiments across tokenizer backbones support the
effectiveness of this design. These results demonstrate the value of combining global compression
with content-adaptive local refinement for compact, high-quality visual representations.
sections.content: 10 Limitations and future work. Although MixTok retains and generates fewer discrete content tokens, reconstruction still requires dense 2D encoding, and the second-stage generator operates on the full spatial grid. Evaluation is currently limited to ImageNet at 256 256 and narrow range of average token budgets. Future work will explore sparse computation and extend adaptive globallocal token allocation to broader budgets, higher resolutions, and more diverse visual data. AI use statement We used generative AI tools, primarily Codex, to assist with method implementation and minor refinements, experimental design and parameter selection, debugging, data processing, experiment execution, and metric aggregation. We also used these tools for translation, manuscript revision, literature search, and reference checking. The main methodological advances were proposed by the authors. The authors reviewed and revised the AI-assisted code, checked experimental logs and metrics, consulted original references, and reviewed the manuscript. The authors take full responsibility for the final content of this work, including its claims, code, and reported results. Ethics statement This study uses ImageNet and publicly available pretrained models and does not involve new data collection or studies with human participants. Like other image generation systems, the method may inherit biases from training data and could be misused to produce misleading imagery. These risks should be considered when deploying downstream systems. Reproducibility statement Our method and experimental details are provided in Sections 4 and 5.1 and Appendix A. Source code and configuration files for reconstruction and generation are available at https: //github.com/LCGLiChenge/MixTok. The repository documents the required datasets, pretrained checkpoints, and other external assets. The project page is available at https://lcglichenge. github.io/MixTok-page/. sections.content: A.1 Implementation Details The settings below describe the main TiTokLlamaGen experimental configuration. Spatial expansion G1D, feature alignment P1D, and the generation Embedding Adapter are separate modules with different output spaces. Tokenizer modules. We use TiTok-L-32 [2] with 4,096-entry codebook of 12-dimensional vectors and LlamaGen VQ-16 [31] with 16,384-entry codebook of 8-dimensional vectors. Spatial expansion G1D is initialized from the TiTok decoder backbone and produces 16 16 grid. The feature adapter P1D uses 1 1 projection to 256 channels, two residual convolutional blocks, and final 1 1 projection. Each residual block contains two 3 3 convolutions with GroupNorm and SiLU. The 2D branchs post-quantization projection P2D maps its 8-dimensional codebook vectors to the same 256-channel decoder space. Grid Scorers. The Reconstruction Grid Scorer projects F1D, F2D, their difference, and its absolute value through separate 1 1 convolutions. The base reconstruction is average-pooled to the grid resolution and processed by two 3 3 convolutions with an intermediate SiLU. These five outputs are summed with learned spatial embedding. Three blocks of 3 3 convolution, eight-group GroupNorm, and SiLU precede 1 1 score head. All hidden features have 128 channels. The Generation Grid Scorer uses the same hidden width, three-block trunk, and score head, with single projection of F1D and learned spatial embedding as its input. Generation modules. The Embedding Adapter adds convolutional residual to the 256-channel base grid and projects it to 768 channels. The residual branch uses two 3 3 convolutions with 128 hidden channels and SiLU, followed by zero-initialized 1 1 convolution to 256 channels. final 1 1 projection produces the spatial context embeddings. The 2D generator is initialized from the pretrained Halton-MaskGIT base model [32], with 12 Transformer layers, 12 attention heads, hidden dimension 768, feed-forward dimension 3,072, and dropout 0.1. It retains the full spatial sequence and one register token; sparse refinement restricts the prediction targets and token updates to R. A.2 Reconstruction Training Details A.2.1 Training Schedule Table 6 summarizes the released three-stage recipe. The 1D encoder and quantizer remain frozen throughout. Alignment pretraining optimizes only G1D and P1D, with the complete 2D tokenizer frozen. Fixed-budget training begins with 0.5 epoch of Reconstruction Grid Scorer optimization, then jointly optimizes spatial expansion, feature alignment, the 2D encoding path, the postquantization projection, the image decoder, and the scorer. Adversarial training starts at epoch 1.5, with 0.01-epoch discriminator warm-up. Top-p fine-tuning initializes from the fixed-budget EMA model, retains the discriminator, resets the optimizer, and enables joint and adversarial training from the start. 15 Table 6 Reconstruction training settings for the main configuration. Batch sizes are global across eight GPUs. Dashes denote frozen or inactive modules. The discriminator uses (0.5, 0.9) and constant learning rate. Weight decay is zero for the 2D branch, scorer, and discriminator; biases and normalization parameters are excluded from weight decay. Tokenizer training uses bicubic resizing of the shorter image side to 256 pixels, followed by center crop, without random cropping or flipping. TiTok inputs lie in [0, 1], and LlamaGen inputs lie in [1, 1]. A.2.2 Scorer Supervision and Differentiable Selection Reconstruction Grid Scorer supervision. Let ˆx2D = D(F2D) be the reconstruction using the complete 2D feature grid. We form an auxiliary supervision map from the difference between the base and 2D reconstruction errors: gi = max(cid:8)0, Avg uΩi [MSEch(ˆxbase,u, xu) MSEch(ˆx2D,u, xu)](cid:9) , (17) where Ωi is the image region pooled into grid cell i, and MSEch averages over color channels. The 37.5% of cells with the largest gi values receive binary target 1; the remaining cells receive 0. Binary cross-entropy with the predicted logits defines Lscore. Targets are detached from the computation graph. This map provides local error-reduction supervision; it is proxy for the benefit of replacing an individual grid feature. Budget and binarization penalties are Lbudget = (s 0.375)2, Lbinary = s(1 s), (19) 16 where the averages cover the local minibatch and spatial positions. Fixed-budget training uses hard top-96 mask with sigmoid surrogate of normalized logits, temperature 0.7, and log-odds bias for ratio 0.375. The budget penalties regularize the soft masks during training; evaluation uses hard selection. A.2.3 Loss Alignment pretraining combines image L1, LPIPS [18], feature L1 between F1D and F2D, and feature-moment matching, with weights 1, 0.5, 0.05, and 0.05, respectively. Moment matching sums the L1 differences of per-channel spatial means and standard deviations. For joint fixed-budget and top-p training, the reconstruction objective in Eq. (14) is supplemented with feature and routing losses. Their coefficients are listed in Table 7. DINOv2 [42] ViT-S/14 and CLIP [43] ViT-B/32 provide frozen, normalized image features. We use L1 distances, averaging DINOv2s class-token and patch-token losses. Both backbones receive images resized to 224 224 and normalized using their respective input statistics. The discriminator uses frozen ConvNeXtBase [44] backbone with trainable convolutional heads. Its feature-matching term compares real and reconstructed features using L1 distance. Adversarial training uses hinge discriminator loss and the negative mean fake score for the generator, with LeCam regularization [45] of weight 103 and EMA decay 0.999. A.3.3 Sampling Configuration For the main generation results, the pretrained TiTok MaskGIT uses eight rounds, guidance scale 4.5 with linear guidance scheduling, and randomization temperature 9.5; softmax temperature annealing is disabled. The Generation Grid Scorer selects locations with = 2 and = 0.75. The Halton generator uses eight rounds with an arccos schedule, guidance weight = 3.0, and categorical sampling at temperature 1. Its classifier-free guidance combines logits as ℓcfg = (1 + w)ℓcond wℓuncond. The mask-token logit is excluded from sampling, and the context embeddings use scale 1. Thus, the final 1D/2D guidance settings are 4.5/3.0, with 8 + 8 sampling rounds. 18 A.4 Evaluation Details Reconstruction. Validation uses the center-crop implementation supplied with LlamaGen and the EMA tokenizer weights. The final allocation parameters are = 1 and = 0.994897, with no additional minimum or maximum token clamp. The threshold was calibrated on randomly sampled subset of the ImageNet training set after the 20-epoch fixed-budget stage to match the target average budget of approximately 96 2D tokens. These evaluation settings differ from the top-p fine-tuning values = 2 and = 0.91 in Table 6. For rFID, original and reconstructed images are clipped to [0, 1], scaled by 255, rounded to uint8, and evaluated with 2,048-dimensional Inception features through TorchMetrics. PSNR is computed for each image in [0, 1] before averaging over the validation set; it is not computed from single dataset-averaged MSE. Reconstruction baseline configurations. We use PyTorch 2.10.0 with CUDA 12.8, four CPU threads per process, TF32 enabled, and cuDNN benchmarking. We retain each implementations attention kernels, caches, guidance, and sampling loops, without torch.compile or CUDA Graphs. BF16 autocast is enabled while preserving explicit precision settings: MixToks latent decoder, scorer, and RGB decoder use FP32, and AdaGens backbone uses internal FP16 autocast. All models are benchmarked sequentially on the same RTX 5090, each in separate process, on shared host with unlocked GPU clocks. These measurements describe the tested implementations and workload; gFID values come from the separate evaluations described in Appendix A.4. FLOPs and parameters. We count one complete class-207, seed-4 inference with PyTorchs FlopCounterMode, counting multiply-add as two FLOPs. The counts include matrix multiplications, convolutions, supported attention operations, all sampling rounds, classifier-free guidance, and final image decoding. Elementwise operations, sorting, sampling, and data movement are excluded from FLOPs but included in latency. FLOPs are reported per image and are not averaged over the 50,000-image quality evaluations. Parameter counts for measured models include all parameters in the instantiated generators and auxiliary generation modules, excluding tokenizers. AdaGen includes its policy network; MixTok includes both generators, its scorer, and adapter. TiTok-S-128 and One-D-Piece-L-256 contain 294.991M and 177.374M parameters under this counting convention, respectively. Halton-L uses its native 384 384 output and is not matched-resolution compute comparison.
